articles.title: Another failed strategy?
articles.content: PRESIDENT Donald Trump’sdeclaration of economic waron Iran is likely to backfire just like his bombing campaign failed to force Iran to surrender. It also exposed the limits of US military options. Wrapped in hyperbolic language, his threats to impose the “toughest sanctions in history” and “the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country” were met with defiance by Tehran. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed them, saying “We have seen this movie before”. Iranian officials warned of halting all oil flows from the Gulf and delivering an “earthquake-like” retaliation if Washington followed through. On what US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Economic D-Day last week, he announced measures to sever Iran’s “financial lifelines” and force a “regime endgame”. But earlier, Trump telephoned Pakistan’s chief of defence forces, Field Marshal Asim Munir and asked him to persuade Iran to resume negotiations. FM Munir thenheaded to Tehran for talkswith Iranian leaders. For all his blusterous rhetoric about “crippling Iran” the outreach was another sign of Trump’s desperation for a deal to end the six-month-old conflict. His flailing actions showed his growing frustration with a deeply unpopular war in his country. According to officials, Pakistan urged Trump to allow time for diplomacy to produce results. Even as mediation efforts got underway, the Trump administration went ahead with the announcement to ratchet up “unprecedented” pressure on Iran and compel it to return to the negotiating table. Iranian officials responded by saying they were “fully prepared” to counter the sanctions, which were an “act of state and economic terrorism”. Bessent widened the scope of economic sanctions against Iran but offered few details of what he called ‘Operation Economic Outcast’. Sanctions targeted Iran’s digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors. It involved action against 60 entities, individuals and vessels. Alongside the financial measures Treasury Secretary Bessent warned the US would punish and isolate countries that continued to trade with Iran and had dealings with its financial system. His ‘either you are with us or against us’ mantra had a wearingly familiar ring. Trump had already issued the same ultimatum, threatening economic penalties against any country doing business with Iran. Tehran responded in kind. It warned that any state, including its neighbours, that joined US economic warfare would be treated as “an enemy”. Trump’s economic warfare will be as futile as his bombing campaign to force Iran to surrender. Bessent said Trump would be phoning some world leaders to ask them to cease their financial interactions with Tehran. But he named no target countries for secondary sanctions. Nor did he say what the penalties would be or specify any timeline for enforcement. No immediate action was taken against Iran’s biggest trading partners. That suggested that the door to de-escalation was being kept open. In any case, it was hardly the first time the tool of sanctions was deployed. Iran has been under multiple US sanctions for four decades and survived them. It seems ready to absorb the pain from this round too. It was also not the first time Trump targeted Iran’s trading partners. Before the war began, he announced tariffs on countries with business ties to Iran. The plan fizzled out and was soon overtaken by theUS-Israeli military assaulton Iran. For now, only the UAE hasdeclareda halt to trade and financial transactions with Iran. This was before Bessent’s announcement and ostensibly in response to ballistic missiles being fired at it, which Iran denied. The suspension will add to Iran’s troubles with its fragile economy facing high inflation and a weakening currency. But it is unclear how and the extent to which the Emirati decision will be enforced. Qatar described US sanctions as unilateral and called instead for mediation efforts. The US depends on the cooperation of other nations to achieve the goals of its punitive economic campaign. China has already pushed back saying pressure tactics won’t work. After Bessent’s threat, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said China “will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own interests” from “illegal unilateral sanctions”. Beijing warned of retaliation if the US imposes secondary sanctions. Washington is unlikely to go beyond threats and want a showdown with its biggest trading partner, especially with a Trump-President Xi Jinping summit coming up next month in Washington. Too much is at stake in that relationship to risk that. The US expectation that countries will fall in line assumes they will give preference to ingratiating themselves with Washington over their own economic interests. This will turn out to be another miscalculation. Many analysts also see it as unsustainable and resting on mistaken assumptions. As Robert Kagan writes inThe Atlantic, “nations that depend on access to the strait — Japan and South Korea, for example — will have to choose between access to a reliable energy supply and participation in American-backed sanctions”. It is improbable they will choose solidarity with Trump’s Washington over their economic interests. He also points out that “the idea that, having survived both military strikes and sanctions, Iran will now succumb to sanctions alone is deluded”. At the same time, mediation efforts by Pakistan and Gulf countries are intensifying and making headway, according to credible reports. This suggests the warring sides haven’t given up on diplomacy. Behind the tough rhetoric of both countries, backchannel communication is aimed at getting negotiations restarted. Tehran wants the US to affirm and abide by the Memorandum of Understanding. Trump wants the Strait of Hormuz to reopen. Iran is reportedly preparing to submit its conditions for reopening the strategic waterway to mediators. The regional mediation initiative aims to first secure a ceasefire, followed by the prompt reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the termination of the US blockade. Whether this can be achieved in coming days remains to be seen. What seems clear is that Trump’s hope that America’s financial muscle will give him victory over Iran will prove to be as futile as his use of military might. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: New units
articles.content: THE debate onnew provincesrests on two different levels. The first is the broader technocratic concern with decentralisation and its hypothetical impact on social welfare and economic growth outcomes. The second is the political economy of constitutional and administrative reform in divided polities. Both aspects are important and it is revealing which one is highlighted by whom and at what point. Let’s start with the first one. Recent research presents a nuanced, but positive leaning relationship between decentralisation reforms and human development/welfare outcomes. In an influential 2016 review article, Channa and Faguet found that decentralisation of health and education spending tends to improve sectoral outcomes, though quality of evidence varies considerably across different cases. Miranda-Lescano et al. (2023) found that decentralising subnational government spending (especially health) positively affects HDI across 57 countries (2000-18). They argue further that such welfare/HDI effects have been understudied relative to growth and governance. The key here is the type of decentralisation that takes place. Reviews of the fiscal decentralisation literature (such as Canare 2021) suggest that revenue decentralisation and fiscal independence, ie, local governments’ ability to raise their own revenue rather than depend on central transfers, are most consistently associated with better development outcomes, while expenditure decentralisation shows no clear pattern. On a cautionary note, there is some evidence to suggest that in weakly governed contexts, usually characterised by low levels of bureaucratic efficiency and transparency, the proliferation of administrative units may also hamper developmental processes, including those associated with economic growth. The discourse in Pakistan needs to take cognisance of what it hopes to primarily achieve through decentralisation. Overall, the picture that emerges is that the right type of decentralisation varies by country, though once in place, it can lead to important gains in development. For a context like Pakistan, the right type of decentralisation would necessarily include not just administrative devolution, but also fiscal devolution. Local governments at whatever tier they work should have the ability to raise revenue and control expenditure, including expenditure on human resource (ie, bureaucrats and other public sector workers). The discourse in Pakistan, regulated as it is from the top down, has fluctuated between reworking provincial boundaries or elevating divisions as ‘administrative units’ with expanded control over various governance aspects. What it is unable to do in clear terms is establish the clear case behind why devolution is needed at this stage. If the primary impetus is to improve social welfare/human development outcomes (ie, outcomes in health and school education), then we may have to come up with a distinct form of devolution. If the impetus is to enable more productive use of capital and labour (ie, catalyse economic growth and transformation), the system that comes out might end up looking a lot different. For more effective human development, Evans and Heller (2015) make an important argument that states require a greater degree of embeddedness with disadvantaged groups in order to deliver the type of welfare gains needed by them. In other words, this means a form of decentralisation that is accountable and participatory at the local level, and one that can avoid the pitfall of local elite capture by propertied groups or by unaccountable bureaucrats. Alternatively, for catalysing economic outcomes, East Asia’s experience suggests that close ties between state and capital, along with high levels of bureaucratic efficiency and autonomy, are necessary to deliver higher rates of growth. China’s decentralisation in the contemporary era, for example, is not necessarily built for the expansion of human capabilities, but rather guiding local capital, and thus it takes a very different form altogether. The discourse in Pakistan (that pitches technocratic reform) needs to take cognisance of what it hopes to primarily achieve through decentralisation. The form of decentralisation and the requisite level that it would have to be aimed at would then flow from this first clarity. In the present it appears the urge for new provinces or even elevating divisions to some as yet unspecified form of administrative unit is driven by political exigency rather than a purpose-led attempt to reform governance. This brings us to the second level of the issue, which is the political economy of reform. The opposition to new provinces or related administrative rejigging rests on both identity-based but also political grounds. Sindhi nationalists speak about the dilution of Sindhi identity and the denial of resources if Karachi is separated. PTI leaders talk about the questionable mandate of the government to undertake a step of this nature. Both of these are not some exceptional or unique forms of opposition. Ethnolinguistic nationalism is an oppositional force in this country as it is in many others. While I personally don’t see how the creation of new administrative units (without any demographic change) can dilute a linguistic identity, it remains a popular position in Sindh and one that has to be reckoned with through politics. The PTI’s response also appears quite decisive in this instance. Change that is introduced under questionable conditions, and with limited legitimacy to back it, is precarious and transient. This is exactly what has plagued previous attempts at devolution or admin reconfiguration, including the 2001 local government ordinance. Ultimately, popular opposition to the manner of implementation makes a worthwhile idea seem worthless as well. The reversal of local governments happened because while they were popular with citizens and local political workers, it was very easy to paint them as the illegitimate engineering attempts of a dictator. Under this reasoning, provincial political elites were able to cement their own type of governing arrangement and recreate centralised rule in the provinces. A similar risk is posed if large-scale administrative change is pushed both without purpose-led clarity and in the face of popular opposition. Fiscally empowered local governments under the provinces, with reasonable judicial or even constitutional protections, might be the most appropriate concession at this stage. And one that may prove to be more sustainable even after the incumbent regime exits. The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums.
articles.author: Umair Javed

articles.title: China-India thaw?
articles.content: IN a few days, Islamabad should closely watch the BRICS summit unfold in New Delhi. Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to attend. The visit would be his first to India in seven years, and signal a meaningful China-India detente since the border clashes of 2020. China’s Vice President Han Zheng last year said the two countries must perform a “dragon-elephant tango”. Can the two Asian powers dance to the same music? A BRICS within which China and India can cooperate — and which is marking the 20th year since its establishment — could offer a formidable counterpoint to the G7. The expanded bloc accounts for 45 per cent of the world’s population and around 35pc of global GDP. But even with Beijing and New Delhi on side, BRICS’ scale and diversity hinders it from being a coherent Global South node in the multipolar world order. Member countries are too geographically and economically disparate to have shared currencies or FTAs, beyond agreeing to partially de-dollarise the world economy. They diverge on key geopolitical issues, global policy frameworks, and pending UN resolutions, limiting the bloc’s influence. The bloc’s anti-Western leanings have been tempered under India’s chairmanship this year. The September meeting will also feel the strains of bringing Iran and the UAE together against the backdrop of a prolonged Middle Eastern conflict. As such, this meeting serves as a staging ground to enable the China-India thaw. That thaw has been underway since last year, when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Xi in Tianjin on the sidelines of the SCO summit. Senior government officials have subsequently met at intervals to discuss trade ties and border security. What unfolds at the BRICS summit will matter to Pakistan. But Xi’s visit to India, if it goes ahead, may not mark a major rapprochement. The two powers will instead seek to establish a well-managed rivalry, recognising the need for pragmatism in a world gone mad, and particularly in the face of US President Donald Trump’s caprices, specifically erratic trade tariffs. As Sanchari Ghosh put it in a recent piece, for India and China, “restoring diplomatic dialogue and practical cooperation does not require restoring trust. India appears to be embracing a form of competitive coexistence, accepting China as a long-term rival while maintaining enough engagement to prevent competition from hardening into perpetual confrontation”. India’s priority will be balancing trade ties so as to tackle the $100 billion trade deficit, and access Chinese goods while reducing its dependency on Chinese imports, particularly in critical sectors such as solar and electronic components. India wants technology transfer, which China is not keen on — for Beijing, long-term ties would depend on India being a stable export market. The result is a hesitant openness on New Delhi’s part: India maintains caps on Chinese ownership and the government must vet proposed Chinese investments. A likely outcome of the meet is better engagement on border security, critical to both countries at a time when they have other preoccupations and the wider region is destabilised. Any thaw should enable data sharing and other cooperation in the context of climate change, including disaster management coordination, an urgent topic as evidenced by the horrific flash flood in the border region of Nepal and China. There is also potential for the China-India thaw to reopen consideration of Pakistan’s BRICS membership. Islamabad expressed interest in joining the bloc in 2023, though its membership has been pending due to Indian opposition. Perhaps Beijing’s advances with New Delhi could influence this conversation, particularly as BRICS chairing responsibilities transition from India to China next year. Pakistan should continue to pursue BRICS membership, as the bloc offers opportunities for interaction with key regional players, and could open new low-tariff South-South trade opportunities (though expectations in this regard are to be managed: Pakistan already exports to many BRICS nations, and would have to significantly boost competitiveness and diversify its exports to benefit markedly). Islamabad would also have to balance BRICS ties with its Western market exposure, including access to schemes such as Europe’s GSP+, and recent engagement with the US on AI data centres and critical mineral supply chains. Multipolarity means that non-Western groupings are proliferating, whether in the form of BRICS Plus or more strategic alliances such as the recent Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. The volume of such South groupings diminishes their geopolitical heft, but participation in them indicates diplomatic and strategic fluidity, a must in increasingly unpredictable times. For that reason alone, what unfolds in New Delhi during Xi’s visit will matter to Islamabad. The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.
articles.author: Huma Yusuf

articles.title: The HKH crisis
articles.content: NEPAL’S deadly glacier-triggered flood in the Himalaya-Karakoram-Hindukush (HKH) region is not a freak disaster. It is a warning that climate change is turning the region’s water tower into a source of systemic economic and security risk. The devastating flood triggered by a glacier collapse that struck the Himalayan region on Aug 26, 2026, severely impacted border areas in Nepal and China (Tibet region) resulting in massive casualties. This is more than a Nepalese tragedy. It is a warning to every government in South Asia. For decades, the Hindu Kush-Himalaya has experienced glacial lake outburst floods, or Glofs. The 1985 Dig Tsho outburst in Nepal, the Bhutan catastrophe of Lugge Tsho flood in 1994 and the 2013 Kedarnath disaster in India demonstrate again how rapidly water, sediment and unstable mountain terrain can turn into mass death. But the danger is changing. A new ICIMOD report confirms that HKH glaciers are losing ice at double the rate since 2000. For too long, however, South Asia has treated the mountains as scenery rather than infrastructure. That is a dangerous mistake. The HKH is often called the world’s Third Pole because it contains the largest concentration of snow and ice outside the Arctic and Antarctic. It is also Asia’s water tower: 10 major river systems originate here and their waters sustain roughly 1.9 billion people downstream. The latest science shows that Himalayan glaciers are losing ice at roughly twice the rate observed around the beginning of this century. On current emissions pathways, the region could lose up to 80 per cent of its present glacier volume by 2100. Even if warming is held to 1.5 to two degrees Celsius, losses of 30-50pc are projected. The implications are profound. In the near term, more melting can mean more water and expanding glacial lakes. Later, as glaciers shrink, the same rivers may carry less meltwater. At the same time, unstable slopes, thawing permafrost, intense rainfall and changing snowfall can increase floods and landslides. The region is therefore moving towards a dangerous paradox: too much water when societies cannot absorb it, and too little when they desperately need it. The Nepal disaster offers a glimpse of the price. The region is moving towards a dangerous paradox. Now look downstream. Pakistan’s repeated urban flooding provides another part of the same warning. Intense monsoon rainfall is increasingly colliding with cities built around drainage systems, land-use decisions and infrastructure designed for yesterday’s climate. Pakistani authorities have repeatedly warned of urban flooding in cities including Lahore, Rawalpindi and others as heavy rains intensify. The lesson is uncomfortable: climate disasters are not produced by climate alone. They are produced when a changing hazard meets weak governance. South Asia therefore needs to stop treating climate adaptation as a collection of national projects. The rivers are regional. The glaciers are regional. The risks are regional. Governance must become regional too. A practical starting point would be a Third Pole Risk Compact: a permanent system connecting glacier and lake monitoring, satellite data, hydrological forecasting, early-warning systems, hydropower operators and disaster-management agencies across the HKH. Artificial intelligence and increasingly cheap sensors could allow warnings to travel across borders in minutes rather than after a disaster has begun. That requires trust and data-sharing among countries that do not always agree on much else. It also requires climate finance to move beyond declarations and into monitoring stations, resilient infrastructure, community preparedness and transboundary early-warning systems. The political argument is equally simple. Business as usual is no longer a neutral cho-ice. It is a risk decision. The warning from Nepal comes just weeks before governments gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for COP31. The conference must recognise that the Third Pole is not a remote environmental concern. It is central to Asia’s water security, food security, energy security and economic stability. A useful way to think about the HKH is as South Asia’s natural balance sheet. Its glaciers are assets. Its rivers are infrastructure. Its forests and wetlands are protective capital. When those assets are degraded, the losses eventually appear on national balance sheets. The choice is now before South Asia’s leaders. They can continue governing as if tomorrow will resemble yesterday or prepare for the climate that is actually arriving. The glacier that collapsed in Nepal did not respect a border. Neither will the next flood, drought or water crisis. The Third Pole is warning us that the future will not unpack like the past. South Asia should listen before it has to pay an even bigger price.
articles.author: Aisha Khan

articles.title: Six months on
articles.content: IT has been six months since the US and Israellaunched their war on Iran— a costly misadventure that remains far from being resolved. In fact, the threat of renewed hostilities is ever-present, despite efforts by regional states, such asPakistan,OmanandQatar, to revive peace talks. The war has been a miscalculation of Trumpian proportions, and the US president and his coterie of war hawks have few ‘good’ options to save face and bring their troops home. Despite the decimation of its religious, political and military top tier in the first few days of the conflict, Iran — which is militarily no match for the US war machine — managed to defend itself, and now conservative factions within the Iranian establishment are unwilling to back down. Rather, they seem prepared to absorb the pain and play the long game with the Americans. Yet instead of realising that the kinetic option has failed against Tehran, the US hasstepped up its economic waragainst the Islamic Republic, warning sovereign states not to do business with Iran. While this action will impact the Iranian economy — which has survived sanctions for over four decades — it is unlikely to make Tehran raise the white flag, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying, “pressure doesn’t work”. Moreover, China, the world’s second biggest economy and a major trading partner of Iran,is not buying it. As the Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said, Beijing “opposes illegal, unilateral sanctions”. Just as the US failed to defeat Iran on the battlefield, it may also fail on the economic front. Wise nations learn from mistakes. But while wisdom may admittedly be in short supply in the White House at the moment, it is time the US put aside its ego and committed itself to finding a diplomatic solution with Iran. The nuclear issue consists of hype more than any credible Iranian threat, while the Strait of Hormuz blockade by Iran is a direct result of the US aggression, with Tehran using the key waterway as a bargaining chip to secure its interests and security. TheIslamabad MoUcontinues to offer the best available off-ramp to all sides, and both Washington and Tehran should return to the spirit of this document. The Iranian president has reaffirmed his country’s belief in dialogue; it is time President Donald Trump did the same. Instead of playing global policeman, the US should re-evaluate its role in the Middle East. Let regional states — specifically Iran and the Arabs — reach a mutually acceptable security framework. If there is to be long-term peace in the region, the US and Israel must end their armed aggression against sovereign states, and allow the people of the region to work out solutions amongst themselves.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Underused gateways
articles.content: THE ADB’s newly approved $400m BUILD facility is a welcome investment in a problem that the Central Asia Regional Economic Cooperation member nations, including Pakistan, have long neglected: the poor state of border crossings. The facility will modernise crossings along the CAREC corridors, replacing ageing infrastructure and manual procedures with digital clearance, better facilities and coordinated border management. The goal is right. Efficient borders can reduce the time and cost of moving goods and people and strengthen Pakistan’s position as a trade and transit route to Afghanistan and Central Asia. As ADB vice-president Leah Gutierrez observed, borders should be gateways to jobs and regional markets, not merely checkpoints. But infrastructure is only half the equation. Pakistan’s bigger problem is that there is remarkably little regional trade to move across its borders. Trade with the five Central Asian republics, for example, fell by more than half in FY26, from almost $444m to $219m. Even the earlier level was tiny for a country seeking to become a regional trade and transit hub. The pattern extends across the neighbourhood. Trade with Afghanistan has been disrupted by border closures and poor relations. Commerce with Iran is negligible, and informal, constrained by US sanctions on Tehran. Trade with India has been largely suspended since 2019. China is the only exception. This leaves Pakistan investing in connectivity while remaining poorly connected economically to the markets around it. The problem is that the ADB can finance scanners, customs systems and border infrastructure but it cannot resolve disputes, mend bilateral ties or remove sanctions. A modern crossing is useless when the border is closed. This is not an argument against BUILD. It is an argument against mistaking infrastructure for regional trade policy. Pakistan should use the facility to make its borders faster, cheaper and more predictable, while addressing the barriers that keep them underused. Islamabad needs an honest assessment of which constraints are unavoidable and which are self-imposed. Political and security concerns may limit regional commerce, but prolonged closures, unpredictable trade policies and bureaucratic obstacles are choices. Pakistan needs better borders. But unless it also creates the conditions for more trade, it will only build gateways to markets it cannot reach.
articles.author: Editorial
